newsitem.title: CHINA: Deng was difficult partner for United States.
newsitem.headline: Deng was difficult partner for United States.

text.p: In 1979, the U.S. magazine Time named Deng Xiaoping its "Man of the Year" and the U.S. media gave giddy reviews to his American tour.

In a whirlwind seven days the diminutive Deng mingled with moguls in Washington and donned a 10-gallon cowboy hat in a Texas rodeo, personifying for many in the United States the cuddly side of communism -- a panda in contrast to the aggressive Soviet bear.

Fast forward to 1989, and Deng's deeds again dominated U.S. front pages -- only this time he was dubbed the "Butcher of Beijing" for ordering the slaughter of hundreds of unarmed pro-democracy demonstrators around Tiananmen Square.

Deng's descent from darling to demon in U.S. popular consciousness mirrored the vicissitudes of his country's difficult diplomatic dance with the United States, a nation China can no more easily live with than live without.
Respect him or revile him, the 5 ft (152 cm) tall Deng loomed large in Sino-U.S. relations and may continue to do so long after his death.

"Deng Xiaoping may well be the last Chinese Communist leader to leave a personal imprint upon the making of Chinese foreign policy," wrote British Sinologist Michael Yahuda in "Deng Xiaoping: Portrait of a Chinese Statesman."

Building on the 1972 diplomatic breakthrough between Mao Zedong and U.S. President Richard Nixon, Deng set the terms of the normalisation of Sino-U.S. diplomatic relations in 1979. In symbolically important gestures, he helped allow the first Coca-Cola and the first Charlie Chaplin films to enter China.

It was a trip to New York in 1974 to address the U.N. General Assembly that opened Deng's eyes to the yawning gap between capitalist prosperity and Communist China's backwardness and sharpened his interest in economic reforms.

During the Sino-U.S. honeymoon, Deng elevated his country's geopolitical profile by playing to U.S. Cold War concerns, going so far as to call in 1979 for a Washington-Beijing alliance against the Soviet Union.
But Deng was no diplomat -- Henry Kissinger once called him "a nasty little man", and Margaret Thatcher, known for her toughness, recoiled from his crudeness.

Deng's major achievement in Sino-U.S. and international relations stemmed from domestic success at economic reforms that irreversibly engaged China with the world after decades of Maoist xenophobia and diverted his people's energies from destructive class struggle to commerce.

However, the late leader's breakthroughs in the vital Sino-U.S. relationship were undermined by what he left unfinished -- his failure to allow political reform commensurate with economic liberalisation and a related inability to accept China's interdependence with the world economy.

"Deng regarded the clamour about human rights abuses in his country as less a sign of the existence of international norms of behaviour than as evidence of a dark plot by Western forces to undermine socialism in China," wrote Yahuda.

Under Deng, U.S. hopes for a broad engagement and Beijing's evolution to a benign power have collided with a Chinese foreign policy of naked nationalism that is hyper-jealous of its sovereignty and seeks maximum gain from the world system at minimum cost, experts say.

Deng's world view was formed under a combination of humiliation at China's 19th century weakness and the raw nationalism that was the global norm in the first part of the 20th century, say Sinologists David Goodman and Gerald Segal.

"This legacy of a man and his country caught in a time warp will pose a fundamental challenge to Deng's successors and to the world outside China," wrote Goodman and Segal in the 1995 monograph "China Without Deng."

As Deng's anointed but insecure successors circled the wagons around their administration in anticipation of the paramount leader's demise, China and the United States clashed on everything from Taiwan to trade and human rights -- but seldom solved their problems.

If part of the friction was due to policy zigzags in Washington, at the core of misunderstanding was a Dengist China that wanted the economic benefits that its open door brought, but dismissed fundamental U.S. values as undesirable "flies" to be filtered out or killed.

"A recurring problem in Sino-American relations has been that rhetoric has exceeded performance, that there has been more thunder than beneficial rain," Jimmy Carter, the first U.S. president to deal with Deng's China, lamented in 1981.
